newsitem.title: UK: Bhutto call for international mediation on Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto call for international mediation on Kashmir.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, warning that Kashmir was a potential flashpoint in South Asia and a threat to regional security, called for international mediation on the disputed territory.
In a speech to the International Institute of Strategic Studies she said it was not a territorial problem, but part of an unfinished issue from the partition of India in 1947.

"I urge you to help find a solution to this problem which has brought untold suffering and which has so deeply and adversely affected the social and economic development of both India and Pakistan," she told the think tank.
As she spoke in a central London hotel, about 50 protesters, some carrying flags and placards saying "Stop our Ethnic Cleansing" and "War Criminal Benazir Bhutto", demonstrated loudly outside.
Bhutto accused India of building up a stockpile of nuclear material but said she was still optimistic that relations between the two countries could improve.
The only obstacle in better ties, she added, is the former Himalayan principality of Kashmir.
Two of the three wars the two countries have fought since independence have been over the former kingdom. But Bhutto, 43, added that there was no need for any historical antagonism.
Predominantly Hindu India controls two thirds, called Jammu and Kashmir, its only Moslem-majority state. The remainder, ruled by Moslem Pakistan, is known as Azad (Free) Kashmir.

"We regard it as an unavoidable aspect of our own destny that we do not accept the denial of the right of self-determination to the people of Jammu and Kashmir and its continued occupation by India," Bhutto said.

India has accused Pakistan of arming and training Kashmiri militants after an uprising against the government in New Delhi broke out in January 1990. Pakistan says it provides only diplomatic support.

When asked how her government would react to the new Taleban radical Islamic militia in Afghanistan which executed former President Najibullah last week, Bhutto said she hoped to have a "positive exchange of views."
"It is our hope, our attempt, our endeavour to be a moderating influence in Afghanistan."

Bhutto's visit to Britain came amid growing internal problems in Pakistan. Last week her estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto and seven other members of his breakaway Shaheed Bhutto faction of the Pakistan's People's Party (PPP) were killed in a shootout with police in Karachi.
His supporters have accused the police of ambushing and killing Murtaza but police claim they fired in self-defence after Murtaza's bodyguards started shooting.

Bhutto, who also met Prime Minister John Major during her brief visit, is due to fly to the United States where she will address the United Nations General Assembly, the Organization of Islamic Conference (OIC) Foreign Ministers Conference and the OIC Contact Group on Kashmir.
